analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and doctors to disclose out-of-network charges and get consent before surprise billing, and caps the charges when they don't.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by two Democratic senators weeks before the 2018 election, was referred to the Senate health committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the practice of surprise medical billing: a patient goes to a hospital that is in their insurance network, gets treated by a doctor or lab that is not, and receives a bill for hundreds or thousands of dollars that insurance will not cover. It would have required hospitals and providers to tell patients in advance whether they are out of network, what the extra charge will be, and get the patient's signed consent at least 24 hours beforehand. If a provider skipped that process, or billed a patient for same-day or emergency care, the patient could only be charged what they would have paid if the provider were in network. The bill also would have set up an arbitration process to settle payment disputes between insurers and out-of-network providers, and made complying with these rules a condition of taking Medicare.
analysis.who_benefits: People with employer-based or other group health insurance who would otherwise get hit with unexpected out-of-network bills — typically after emergency care, or when an anesthesiologist, radiologist, or lab at an in-network hospital turns out to be out of network. The bill also guaranteed that whatever a patient pays in a surprise billing situation counts toward their annual out-of-pocket maximum.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured patients facing surprise out-of-network bills

how_it_helps.text: Providers treating patients in group-market plans would have to tell patients on the day they make an appointment and the day of service whether they are out of network, give a written estimate of the extra charge, and get a signed consent form at least 24 hours before furnishing out-of-network care [S3].

If an out-of-network provider fails to give that notice and consent, or bills a patient for same-day or emergency services, the provider could not charge the patient more than the normal in-network cost sharing [S3].
Any amount a patient pays in a surprise billing situation would count toward the plan's annual limit on out-of-pocket costs, closing a gap where surprise bills often did not [S3].

The bill would create an independent arbitration process, run by certified entities screened for conflicts of interest, to settle payment disputes between insurers and out-of-network providers, with decisions based partly on regional in-network rates and Medicare rates [S3].
Hospitals, critical access hospitals, and ambulatory surgical centers would have to adopt and enforce these anti-surprise-billing policies as a condition of participating in Medicare [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Out-of-network hospitals, emergency physicians, and specialists (anesthesiologists, radiologists, pathologists, labs) who currently collect balance bills from patients above what insurance pays. Insurers would take on new payment-dispute obligations, and whichever side loses arbitration pays the full cost of the process.

drawbacks.text: The consent provision creates a loophole: an out-of-network provider who follows the paperwork can still bill a patient well above in-network rates, and a patient signing a form in a stressful situation — or their representative — may not fully grasp the extra charge [S3].
The bill only covers group health plans and group-market insurance, leaving people who buy individual coverage without the same protection [S3].

Hospitals would face compliance costs for new notice, documentation, and recordkeeping requirements, and the loser of an arbitration case pays the entire cost of the process, which could discourage smaller providers from contesting low payment offers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is strong: patients who never chose an out-of-network provider could no longer be charged more than in-network rates. The weaknesses are the consent loophole, which lets providers keep the practice alive by getting signatures, and the restriction to group-market plans only. An honest supporter would acknowledge the paperwork burden on hospitals, but the main cost falls on providers who lose the ability to collect charges patients never agreed to.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Maggie Hassan introduced the bill on October 11, 2018, for herself and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, about four weeks before the 2018 midterm elections [S1].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill's protections would not have taken effect until two years after enactment, so even prompt passage would have delayed relief [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Out-of-network hospitals and physicians kept the ability to bill patients above in-network rates for care they had no chance to agree to in advance. Patients with surprise bills got nothing from this Congress.

for.name: Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the No More Surprise Medical Bills Act of 2018 and referred it to the Senate health committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (Chair Lamar Alexander, R-TN)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no recorded opposition or party breakdown — it was introduced by two Democratic senators and died quietly in a Republican-chaired committee without anyone going on record against it.

industries.industry: Out-of-network hospitals and physician specialists (emergency medicine, anesthesiology, radiology, pathology)
industries.note: These providers collect balance bills from patients far above what insurers pay, often when the patient had no way to know they were out of network. The bill would have capped those charges at in-network cost sharing whenever the provider skipped notice and consent, or in same-day and emergency situations. Their interest in keeping surprise billing runs directly against patients' interest in not receiving the bills.

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plans
industries.note: Insurers would gain a structured arbitration process and be shielded from providers passing unchecked charges to their enrollees, but they would also face new obligations: pay out-of-network bills within 30 days or negotiate, and cover the full cost of arbitration whenever they lose one. Their interest in limiting surprise bills generally lines up with patients'.
